title: Book 7 — Polymnia, Chapter 144
paragraphs: Another opinion of Themistocles had already, at the right moment, proved to be the best. The Athenians had had large sums accumulating in the public treasury from the revenue of the mines at Laurium, and were planning to distribute them among themselves, ten drachmas to each man. Themistocles persuaded them to give up this plan of distribution and instead to build with this money two hundred ships for the war — meaning the war with Aegina. For that war, as it turned out, was the salvation of Greece at that time, by compelling the Athenians to become a naval power. The ships, though not used for the purpose for which they had been built, thus proved of service to Greece when Greece needed them. These ships, then, the Athenians already had, having built them beforehand; in addition it was necessary to build others. After the oracle was given, they decided in council to receive with their ships in full force the barbarian invading Greece — following the god's commands — together with those Greeks willing to join them.
